Voices From The Salt Marsh

For thirty years the glasswing ferry crossed between the shingle town and the marsh landing, carrying mail, bicycles, and an unreasonable number of pie tins. Before the causeway closed for repairs, we sat down with two people who know the marsh better than the tide tables do, and asked them what the water has been trying to say all along.

Marta Vell

Marta Vell: I started counting reeds the summer I turned nine, because my grandmother paid me in plum sweets and honest attention. You learn the salt marsh by repetition. The same channel, the same heron, the same smell of sulfur after rain. Strangers see empty mud; I see forty years of neighbors who happen to photosynthesize and never borrow tools without returning them cleaner.

Interviewer: What changed first after the storm season? Marta Vell: Trust changed first, funny enough. The channel moved eighty meters east in one winter and everybody had to renegotiate where the dock went. People who had argued about mooring rights since the seventies suddenly shared hammers, timber, and hot soup, and nobody mentioned the old grievance aloud ever again.

Interviewer: Does the marsh forgive? Marta Vell: The marsh keeps accounts differently. It forgives nothing and forgets nothing, yet it starts over every single spring without complaint. I find that more instructive than most sermons. You step carefully, you repair your own boardwalk, and you assume the mud will be soft exactly where you were sure it was firm.

Deniz Okafor

Deniz Okafor: I mapped the reed beds for the county, season after season, pushing a borrowed canoe and arguing with my own instruments. The beds tripled in twenty years. Everyone credited luck or weather, but the maps show a corridor of patience where grazing stopped and the fence came down. Give a marsh a decade of nobody arguing with it and it will outbuild any restoration crew sent to help.

Interviewer: And the birds came back? Deniz Okafor: Louder than the highway, honestly. First the egrets, then the godwits, then species I had to look up twice with red cheeks. By the fifth spring the dawn chorus had a bassline you could feel through the canoe hull. County officials visited expecting a tidy photograph and left with wet socks and a funding proposal instead.

Interviewer: Any advice for the town? Deniz Okafor: Leave the edge ragged. Concrete edges teach water to be violent; ragged edges teach it manners. Every fallen branch left where it fell is a nursery, a breakwater, and a free lesson in engineering. The marsh repays neglect better than it repays management, and it keeps the receipts for everything else you do to it.

Closing Notes

Both speakers agreed on one thing without hesitation: the salt marsh rewards people who show up repeatedly and expect nothing dramatic. The glasswing ferry resumes service in the spring, the pie tins are already stacked by the landing, and the reeds, as Marta put it, intend to keep the minutes.
